title: Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson (2019)
summary: Home Depot could not remove as a third-party counterclaim defendant under the general removal statute or the CAFA provision considered.
notes:
A strong federal interest or substantial class exposure does not itself supply removal authorization. Begin with statutory party status, then analyze original jurisdiction and the remaining removal requirements.

Citibank sued Jackson in North Carolina state court to collect a debt for a water-treatment system; Jackson counterclaimed against Citibank and added class claims against Home Depot and Carolina Water Systems. The Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit 5-4 in an opinion by Justice Thomas (joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan), reasoning that a third-party counterclaim defendant is a defendant to a claim but not to the 'civil action.'.

sections.Parties: A bank began a debt-collection action against Jackson. Jackson asserted counterclaims concerning the underlying transaction and added Home Depot as a defendant to the counterclaim.
sections.Material Facts: Home Depot entered through the counterclaim, rather than being named as a defendant in the original complaint. The added claims included class allegations. Home Depot argued that its new position defending those claims, together with the Class Action Fairness Act, allowed it to choose a federal forum.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court held that the statutory removal provisions did not authorize Home Depot’s removal in that posture.
sections.Issue: Did being named as a new defendant in a class counterclaim make Home Depot a removing defendant under the statutes?
sections.Holding: No. The general provision referred to defendants in the original civil action, and the CAFA language did not produce a different result here.
sections.Reasoning: The Court read the removal provisions in relation to the action defined by the original complaint. The relevant status was therefore more specific than merely being required to defend a claim. CAFA relaxed several conventional removal restrictions but did not, in the majority’s reading, change this basic identification of who could remove. The result preserves a distinction among original defendants, original plaintiffs facing counterclaims, and newly added counterclaim defendants.

learning.why: Home Depot could not remove as a third-party counterclaim defendant under the general removal statute or the CAFA provision considered.

topics.cp-removal: A third-party counterclaim defendant was outside the relevant removal authorization. Original-party alignment mattered even when the counterclaim introduced a new corporate defendant.
topics.cp-cafa: CAFA’s removal language did not expand the category to this counterclaim defendant.
topics.cp-usc-1441: The holding rests on the meaning of 'defendant' in 1441(a) as the defendant to the original civil action.
topics.cp-usc-1453: The Court also construed CAFA's removal provision, 1453(b), holding 'any defendant' does not expand the class of parties who may remove.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The 5-4 split turned on textual reading of 'defendant' across the removal statutes, a model of jurisdictional-statute interpretation.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Alito, joined by three Justices, dissented from the majority’s reading and its practical consequences for newly added counterclaim defendants.

mnemonic.rationale: A water treatment system on credit
